newsitem.title: USA: Ex-CIA man pleads guilty in latest Moscow spy case.
newsitem.headline: Ex-CIA man pleads guilty in latest Moscow spy case.

text.p: Harold Nicholson, the highest ranking CIA officer ever charged with spying and the second accused U.S. turncoat brought to court in three days, pleaded guilty on Monday to selling secrets to Russia.

Nicholson, 46, was a 16-year veteran of the Central Intelligence Agency's clandestine operations directorate where he had access to the names of spies working for the CIA and other secrets. He was station chief in Romania and deputy chief in Malaysia.
He was the second national security official to plead guilty to spying for Moscow in the past few days.
On Friday, a former FBI counterintelligence agent, Earl Edwin Pitts, pleaded guilty to selling classified information for more than $200,000.
The two latest guilty pleas wrapped up the country's most serious espionage cases since former CIA officer Aldrich Ames was caught spying for Moscow in 1994.

Nicholson was accused of selling national security secrets for 29 months until his November 16 arrest, including the names and planned assignments abroad of new undercover CIA officers. He was allegedly paid more than $180,000 for his information.
His most recent assignment was as a branch chief in the Middle East division of the counterterrorism centre at CIA headquarters.
Chief U.S. District Court Judge James Cacheris accepted Nicholson's plea and set sentencing for June 5.
For entering the plea agreement, Nicholson could get less than a life sentence which he faced if he had been convicted.
Cacheris took Nicholson through a lengthy series of questions to determine that he was freely pleading gulty and fully understood the consequences.
After swearing Nicholson in, the judge asked if he was satisfied with his court-appointed lawyers.
Dressed in a khaki and grey Alexandria jail jumpsuit, Nicholson said: "I'm very satisfied."
Judge Cacheris said: "I find the defendant guilty."
Lawyers for Nicholson sought to keep a gag order in effect, but the judge ruled against them so the case can be discussed freely by prosecutors who planned a press conference later Monday.
